newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK office property mart seen set for firm recovery.
newsitem.headline: HK office property mart seen set for firm recovery.

text.p: Hong Kong's flagging office property market is poised for a firm recovery in 1997 after a major property deal in the heart of the territory's Central district jump-started the market, analysts said on Friday.

Hysan Development Ltd agreed last week to buy a commercial and office block, the Entertainment Building, in the business hub of Hong Kong Island for HK$3.64 billion (US$471 million). The office space was valued at about HK$15,000 per square foot.
"The Hysan deal has provided a benchmark for what conservative, long-term investors believe property is worth," said Janice Wallace, executive director at Goldman Sachs.
"The importance of that deal is that it is a whole building with a very blue chip buyer so it provides a good indication of value."

The last benchmark price seen in the industry was HK$14,000 per square foot for one floor in Nine Queen's Road Central in May. CS First Boston said in a recent report it sees "a flow on effect" from Hysan's purchase of the Entertainment Building.
On Friday, property investment and development company Chi Cheung Investment Co Ltd said it had agreed to sell the 20th floor of Nine Queen's Road Central for about HK$14,917 per square foot.

Euan Weir, analyst at Merrill Lynch, said the Hysan deal had shown a faster and stronger upturn than anticipated. "I think people have been too negative. I think that people have exaggerated the downside," he said.

Analysts said office property values had bottomed out by the second quarter of 1996, and interest from mainland Chinese buyers ahead of the mid-1997 handover of Hong Kong to China had contributed to a lift in prices.

CS First Boston analyst Geoffrey Palmer said in his report that a 10 percent rise in prime office space values over the next 12 months was not unreasonable. "Demand is extremely strong with virtually no large vacant spaces available," he said.
Hong Kong office values in some cases were down more than 50 percent from their peak in mid-1994, CS First Boston said.
While more supply was set to come on stream, analysts said it was unlikely to hit prices before the end of 1997.

"It's some six to nine months down the road," said David Low, research manager at Asia Equity. "For tenants looking for expansion, they probably have to pay current market rates. There is not much room for negotiation."
Weir said that with values rising, rents would also have to increase for property companies to achieve stable yields.
"To get yields similar to the cost of funds, Hysan is pointing to a pick up in rental yields," he said. "I think the situation for 1997 for rentals looks a little bit better."

Analysts said tenants were currently paying about HK$70 per square foot. CITIC Pacific Ltd said on Thursday it would lease its CITIC Tower Grade A office complex in Central for HK$60 to HK$70 per square foot.

"Office rents, which have failed to move in line with values, have only recently stopped declining," CS First Boston said. "We anticipate a relatively quick pickup, with rents in prime areas increasing by about 15 percent next year."
Analysts said significant supply was set to hit the market in 1998, but Edward Chan, research director at NAVA SC Securities, said core locations would continue to be well bid.
"...Central and Admiralty will still be under heavy demand," he said. "We expect about eight to 10 percent growth in office rentals (next year)."
